verdicts.trueWording: Everything quietly, ineluctably fades into history
verdicts.note: Final paragraph of the Dirda review, raw HTML fetched from brightweavings.com (HTTP 200): “‘Under Heaven’ ends where it began, among ghosts. Everything quietly, ineluctably fades into history, as into those mists one sees on Chinese scroll paintings.” Page byline confirms Michael Dirda of The Washington Post, reproduced with permission.

verdicts.trueWording: told with flair, passion and elegant prose
verdicts.note: Final paragraph: “River of Stars (*****) … is told with flair, passion and elegant prose.” Page title/byline confirm Adam Whitehead of The Wertzone and that the book reviewed is River of Stars.

verdicts.trueWording: In six hundred plus pages, not a word of this novel feels gratuitous
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim on the page; the ‘over six hundred pages’ limb is carried by the page’s own ‘In six hundred plus pages’ in the same sentence. Byline confirms Indrapramit Das for Strange Horizons, reviewing River of Stars.

verdicts.trueWording: sentences are often convoluted, meanings often obscured
verdicts.note: In the ‘What to say?’ paragraph, of Kay’s prose: “his style is very involved and requires a certain level of concentration from his reader; sentences are often convoluted, meanings often obscured.” Byline: Victoria Hoyle of Eve’s Alexandria, reviewing Sailing to Sarantium.

verdicts.trueWording: flavoured with an archaism that prompts a second glance and a slower read
verdicts.note: Same paragraph, next sentence: “The phrasing is sometimes flavoured with an archaism that prompts a second glance and a slower read” — the ‘makes the reader slow down’ limb is the page’s own ‘and a slower read’.

verdicts.trueWording: giving us elaborate foreshadowing with a sort of detached amusement
verdicts.note: Paragraph beginning ‘First, Kay likes exercising tricks of the narrator’s trade’. Byline: Joe Milicia, New York Review of Science Fiction, reprinted at BrightWeavings; the book under review is Sailing to Sarantium.

verdicts.trueWording: This, in turn, might have occasioned a significant change in various affairs
verdicts.note: The parenthetical sample of Kay’s text reads: “Had he arrived back at the inn after the racing, as he had intended…, Crispin would almost certainly have conducted himself differently in certain matters that followed. This, in turn, might have occasioned a significant change in various affairs, both personal and of much wider import.” Counterfactual conditional about consequences of an arrival that did not occur; Milicia adds ‘And so on for another whole paragraph.’

verdicts.trueWording: an intricately rearranged chronology and a wittily drawn-out suspense
verdicts.note: Paragraph beginning ‘Kay is also extremely skilled’: “Also brilliant is Kay’s virtuoso handling of structure in the chapter that follows … but all with an intricately rearranged chronology and a wittily drawn-out suspense.” Praise limb (‘Also brilliant’, ‘virtuoso’) and ‘a chapter’ limb both on the page; the reviewed book is Sailing to Sarantium (opening paragraph).

verdicts.trueWording: the long Prologue is a bit plodding
verdicts.note: Parenthetical in the same paragraph: “Kay is also extremely skilled, especially in the later chapters (the long Prologue is a bit plodding), in building a lengthy scene to a dramatic climax.” Book confirmed as Sailing to Sarantium.

verdicts.trueWording: Here is Kay at his most historical, reshaping the reign of Justinian and Theodora
verdicts.note: Paragraph beginning ‘As a first volume’. Header confirms the piece is by Dena Taylor and ‘part of an upcoming book on GGK being published by NIMROD PRESS … in the BABEL HANDBOOKS series’, on Sailing to Sarantium.

verdicts.trueWording: The language in Last Light … is harder, terser, less lyric than the books before
verdicts.note: Answer to question 6: “The language in Last Light , for example, is harder, terser, less lyric than the books before (and some reviewers and scholars have commented on this).” The same page names the book in full as The Last Light of the Sun in several other answers.

verdicts.trueWording: Certainly not a linguistic attempt to echo anyone else.
verdicts.note: Opening of the same answer to question 6, replying to Marcus’s ‘Was this style inspired by anyone in particular’; Kay goes on to describe operatic rhythms and mythic, Biblical cadences in Fionavar as his own device, not an echo of another writer.

verdicts.trueWording: the almost opulence of your language … elevate everything above the mundane
verdicts.note: Question 6, verbatim: “One of the elements I’ve always been particularly fond of … has been the almost opulence of your language. It lends a splendour to events, but it also seems to elevate everything above the mundane.” The page says ‘everything’ where the claim says ‘events’, but ‘lends a splendour to events’ sits in the same sentence, so the limb holds. Header confirms Richard Marcus of ‘Leap in the Dark’ as interviewer.

verdicts.trueWording: you don’t blend colours – you contrast them to form an illusion of blending when you back away
verdicts.note: Answer on the prologue of Sailing to Sarantium written as a mosaic: “That’s the art form of mosaic; you don’t blend colours – you contrast them to form an illusion of blending when you back away. When you get too close you can’t see it clearly…” — the ‘only at a distance’ limb is the page’s ‘when you back away’. Header confirms Peter Halasz, NYRSF, 2000.

verdicts.trueWording: Lions is elegiac in nature because it is really … about the demise of a civilisation
verdicts.note: Answer on style and tone changing between books: “Lions is elegiac in nature because it is really, as much as anything else, about the demise of a civilisation. The demise of the Arab civilisation in Spain.” Same Halasz/NYRSF interview page.
